Guitar Chord Shapes by Hand: From Easy to Hard Fingerings

This lesson orders chord shapes by what the fretting hand finds hard, starting from a first lesson on guitar. Each step adds one physical demand: more fingers, a stretch, a barre, a muted string, a shift along the neck. Each step says what makes the shape easy, what makes it hard, and what usually goes wrong. Guitar chord shapes has the same chords in harmonic order, from pop toward jazz.

How to read the diagrams. The neck stands upright, with string 6 (low E) on the left. Each dot shows its chord tone, R for the root. The numbers under each diagram are the frets from low E to high E, and x is a string you don’t play. Fingers are numbered 1 (index) to 4 (little finger). Press ▶ to hear a shape.

Finger numbers and barres. The button below puts the finger numbers in the dots instead of the chord tones, on every diagram on the page. Where one finger lies across several strings, a shaded bar joins those dots. The bar is drawn only where a barre is new: the small barre in G-B6, the first full barres in G-B8 and G-B9, and the barre with a silent string in G-B13. Tick the box to draw it on every diagram.

Finger numbers on guitar and on piano. The two instruments count differently. On guitar the thumb is not counted: the index finger is 1, then middle 2, ring 3 and little finger 4, and a thumb fretting a bass note over the top of the neck is written T. On piano the thumb is 1 and the little finger 5, and the left hand is numbered the same way as the right, so its little finger plays the lowest note. A “3” is the ring finger to a guitarist and the middle finger to a pianist. Picking-hand fingers on guitar have letters of their own (p, i, m, a), so they are never mixed up with these.

Hand position

Good position is what makes every shape below easier, so set it up before the first chord and check it again whenever a shape feels hard.

  • Thumb: behind the neck, roughly opposite finger 2, with the pad (not the flat of the thumb) on the wood. It is a rest to push against, not a clamp. Squeezing harder does not make the note clearer.

  • Fingertips: arch each finger so that the tip comes down on the string from above, just behind the fret wire (the side towards the tuning pegs). Close to the fret needs the least pressure and buzzes least. The middle of the gap between frets needs more pressure and still buzzes.

  • Fingers: curved, with the knuckle joints bent. A curved finger lets the strings next to it ring.

  • Wrist and elbow: the wrist stays fairly straight, not bent sharply down or back, and the elbow hangs relaxed instead of pinned to the ribs or lifted. The palm stays a little away from the neck, so there is a gap you could slide a finger through.

  • Guitar angle: sit with the guitar body against your right thigh and the neck pointing slightly upward. Looking down at the fretboard should not need you to twist your wrist.

  • Easy because: with the thumb behind the neck, the fingers fall on the frets and need very little effort.

  • Hard because: it is not how the hand sits when it rests, so for the first weeks it takes thought.

  • What goes wrong:

    • The thumb climbs over the top of the neck. That makes the fingers flat, and they mute the strings next to them. (An occasional thumb over the top for a bass note is fine: that is the T in the diagrams.)
    • Flat fingers: the pad lies on the string and touches its neighbour.
    • The tip sits in the middle of the fret space, or on the fret wire, and the note buzzes or dies.
    • The wrist collapses and the palm presses on the neck, which is tiring and slows changes.
    • Long nails stop the fingertip landing; trim the fretting hand’s nails short.

Practice: place the fingers of a chord one at a time, checking each tip. Pick the strings one by one. If a string buzzes, move that fingertip closer to the fret before pressing harder.

G-B1 One or two fingers

Em7 takes finger 2. Em uses 2 and 3, and E5 does too, with the higher strings left silent. E7 uses fingers 2 and 1, and Am7 uses 2 and 1.

  • Easy because: one or two fingers, no stretch, and everything is within two frets.
  • Hard because: each finger has to press firmly enough to make a clean note, and the strum has to land on the right strings.
  • What goes wrong:
    • Fingertips hurt for the first week or two.
    • A string buzzes when the finger sits back from the fret instead of just behind it.
    • A fingertip leans on the next string and mutes it.

Practice: hold Em and pick one string at a time, so you can hear that each one rings. Five minutes a day builds calluses.

Unlocks: two-chord strums; G-A1 and G-A2.

G-B2 Three fingers, close together

Am and E are the same shape, moved over one string; both are fingered 2-3-1. A is 1-2-3, or a small index-finger barre across three strings. D is 1-3-2, with finger 1 on string 3, finger 3 on string 2 and finger 2 on string 1. Dm is the same three fingers in a different order, 2-3-1. D7 is 2-1-3: it is D with the middle finger moved to the other side, so the three fingers sit close together as in D.

  • Easy because: the fingers stay together and no finger reaches across another.
  • Hard because: three fingers have to land at once, and in A they crowd into one fret.
  • What goes wrong:
    • In D and D7, finger 3 touches the high E string and mutes it.
    • In A, the fingers collide.
    • Changing between E and A is slow.

Practice: move from Am to E. Fingers 2 and 3 move across one string together, and finger 1 stays on its fret, moving from string 2 to string 3. Go as slowly as you need to keep the shape.

Unlocks: four-chord loops that use only these chords; Boom-chick.

G-B3 Reaching: C and G

C is fingered 3-2-1, from string 5 up to string 2. Cadd9 adds finger 4 on string 2 in place of finger 1. G is 2-1-3, or 3-2-4 with finger 4 on both of the top two strings.

  • Easy because: everything is within the first three frets.
  • Hard because: in C the fingers spread diagonally over three frets and three strings. In G the fingers are far apart across the neck, and the strings between them have to ring open.
  • What goes wrong:
    • In C, finger 1 leans on the high E string.
    • The thumb rides high over the neck, which shortens the reach. Keep it low, behind the neck.

A note on the B string in G. In G the B string rings open, and it sits right beside the finger on the high E string. That finger, finger 3 or 4, can lean back and touch the B string, and then the string goes dull or silent. The chord is still G, because the B on string 5 still sounds, but it is thinner and the strum sounds uneven. To avoid it, press with the tip and keep the knuckle arched. Damping the B string can also be a choice: let the finger on string 1 lie lightly against it, and the chord loses one of its two B’s and sounds more open. The X in the second diagram marks the B string damped.

Practice: form C, lift all three fingers together, and put them down again without looking. Repeat ten times.

Unlocks: C, Am, F, G, and the pop changes of G-A1 and G-A4.

G-B4 Four fingers: open 7ths

C7 is C with finger 4 added on string 3. B7 uses all four fingers in a cluster: 2-1-3-4. Fmaj7 is a small shape on the top four strings.

  • Easy because: each shape is a small change from one you already know.
  • Hard because: four fingers are down at once, including the weak little finger, and B7 is a cramped cluster.
  • What goes wrong:
    • The little finger lands on the pad instead of the tip and mutes the next string.
    • The change from C to C7 is slow because finger 4 starts far away.

Practice: hold C and tap finger 4 on and off string 3, fret 3 (C to C7 and back), without lifting the other fingers.

Unlocks: Blues shuffle and the open-position 12-bar blues; G-A5.

G-B5 Reach: a wide stretch

The reach of a hand is how far apart the fingers can press at once. G7 is G with the little finger’s note moved down: finger 3 on string 6 at fret 3, finger 2 on string 5 at fret 2, and finger 1 on string 1 at fret 1. The fingers sit on the two outer strings and on opposite sides of the neck, so the hand opens as wide as it does in any open chord. Compare it with G above it.

  • Easy because: only three fingers, and the strings between them ring open.
  • Hard because: the hand has to open across all six strings and three frets at the same time. Small hands feel it most.
  • What goes wrong:
    • The thumb creeps up over the neck, which shortens the reach and makes it worse.
    • Finger 1 reaches the high E string at an angle and touches the string next to it.
    • The wrist bends sharply to make up the distance. Keep it fairly straight, with the elbow close to the body.

Practice: form G, then change to G7 by lifting finger 3 and putting down finger 1, with fingers 2 and 3 staying where they are. Do not hurry. If the stretch hurts, stop and rest, and do a little each day. The span grows with patience.

Unlocks: the G7 in blues and country changes; G-A5.

G-B6 Two strings under one finger

In Dm7, finger 1 lies flat across strings 2 and 1 at the first fret. In F, fingers 3 and 2 go down beside that small barre.

  • Easy because: the barre covers only two strings.
  • Hard because: for the first time, one finger presses two strings, and it has to lie flat rather than on its tip.
  • What goes wrong:
    • String 2 is dull because it falls in the crease of the finger. Roll the finger slightly onto its outer edge.
    • The thumb creeps around the front of the neck.

Practice: put finger 1 alone across strings 2 and 1 and pick each string, until both ring. Then add the other fingers.

Unlocks: the F chord in the pop changes.

G-B7 Top-string triads

Moveable shapes. A chord shape can slide up and down the neck as long as it has no open string. An open string stays at the same pitch when the hand moves, so the shape would change. If every note is fretted, the whole shape moves together, and the chord’s name changes with the root. Of the shapes above, C xxx010 and Am xxx210 use open strings and stay where they are. C xxx553, C xxx988 and F xxx565 are fully fretted, so they move. The same is true of the barre chords in G-B8 and G-B9.

Three positions of the same triad. A triad has three notes, and any of them can be the lowest. On strings 3, 2 and 1 these are the moveable shapes. The root is on string 3 in root position, on string 1 in first inversion, and on string 2 in second inversion. Find the root and you know the chord.

In root position the root is the lowest note. In first inversion the 3rd is the lowest, and in second inversion the 5th is. The inversions lesson explains the names and how to write them, and pianists can see the same idea in piano inversions. The next step is voice leading: when you change chords, choose the inversion that is nearest, so each note moves a fret or two, or stays put. That is how a few small shapes on the top strings can follow a whole progression, and it is where this lesson leads.

  • Easy because: only three notes, and at most three fingers.
  • Hard because: strings 6, 5 and 4 must stay silent. Either pick only the top three strings, or let your fretting fingers rest lightly against the low strings to damp them. Higher up the neck the frets get closer together.
  • What goes wrong:
    • The open low strings ring.
    • The pick catches string 4.
    • The chord sounds thin. It is meant to: it is one part in a band.

Practice: play the three C shapes in a loop, picking the strings one at a time and then together.

Unlocks: funk and reggae chops; G-A9.

G-B8 Full barre, E shape

Finger 1 lies across all six strings, and the other fingers make the E shape in front of it: the open E chord, fingered 2-3-4 instead of 1-2-3, moved up so that the barre does the nut’s job. The root is on string 6, under the barre. Here the barre is at fret 5, which makes these A, Am, A7 and Am7.

Start at fret 5, not at F. The usual first barre chord is F, at fret 1, and it is the hardest place to learn it. Near the nut the strings sit highest above the frets and are under the most tension there, so the barre has to press hardest, and the frets are widest, so the hand has to stretch furthest. Around fret 5, closer to the bridge, the strings give more easily and the frets are closer together. Get the shape ringing there, then move it down a fret at a time (A♭, G, G♭) until you reach F. G-B10 does that move on purpose.

  • Easy because: the shape on top of the barre is E, which you already know.
  • Hard because: one finger presses six strings, which takes strength, and the hand tires quickly.
  • What goes wrong:
    • Strings buzz. Put the barre right behind the fret, and roll the finger so that its firmer outer edge, not the soft pad, meets the strings.
    • String 2 or 3 falls in a crease of the finger.
    • The elbow sticks out.
    Fm and Fm7 are a little easier, since they need fewer fingers on top of the barre.

Practice: play the barre alone at fret 5, no other fingers, until all six strings ring. Hold for 10 seconds and rest for 20. Or put a capo at fret 5 and play E shapes above it, then do the capo’s job with your finger. When fret 5 is easy, do the same at fret 3, then fret 1.

Unlocks: every major and minor chord; G-A3.

G-B9 Barre, A shape

The A shape: the open A chord with a barre behind it on string 5, the root under the barre. String 6 is not played. At fret 5 these are D, Dm, Dm7, D7 and Dmaj7; the same shapes at fret 1 are B♭, B♭m and the rest, where the stretch and the pressure are greater for the same reasons as F.

  • Easy because: the barre covers five strings, not six.
  • Hard because: three fingers squeeze into one fret space on adjacent strings. Many players flatten finger 3 across strings 4, 3 and 2 instead, which takes practice of its own.
  • What goes wrong:
    • When finger 3 lies flat, it mutes string 1.
    • Finger 1 bends at the knuckle and lets string 1 go dead.

Practice: play Dm at fret 5 with the barre and finger 3 only, then add fingers 4 and 2. Then move it down to Cm (fret 3) and Bm (fret 2).

Unlocks: barre chords anywhere on the neck.

G-B10 Moving a shape along the neck

The first three are the E shape (root on string 6) at frets 5, 3 and 1: A, G and F. The last three are the A shape (root on string 5) at frets 5, 3 and 2: Dm, Cm and Bm. They are written in that order, from fret 5 down, so that the move takes you from the easy end of the neck toward the hard one. Name the chord by the note under the barre: on string 6 for the E shape, on string 5 for the A shape.

  • Easy because: the shape doesn’t change, only the fret.
  • Hard because: you have to find the new fret without looking, and release just enough pressure to slide without the strings squeaking, all without dropping the beat.
  • What goes wrong:
    • A gap between chords.
    • Landing a fret off.
    • A scrape on the slide. Ease off the pressure, but don’t lift the fingers.

Practice: slide A down to G and back on a steady beat, then G down to F, using the fret markers at 3, 5, 7 and 9 as landmarks.

Unlocks: I–IV–V and the 12-bar blues in barre chords, in any key.

G-B11 Barre 7ths: finger independence

A7 and Am7 are the E shape at fret 5 with a finger taken away, so the barre itself plays the 7th on string 4; F7 is the same at fret 1. D7, Dmaj7 and Cmaj7 are the A shape, with the root on string 5. Learn them at fret 5 first, as in G-B8.

  • Easy because: A7 and Am7 are barres you already know, with a finger taken away.
  • Hard because: the little finger now has to press at the far end of a barre. Cmaj7 x35453 needs fingers 2, 3 and 4 spread across strings 4, 3 and 2.
  • What goes wrong:
    • The little finger collapses and mutes a neighbouring string.
    • It hasn’t the strength yet.

Practice: hold a barre and tap finger 4 on one string, fret by fret.

Unlocks: Bossa nova in barre positions; G-A6.

G-B12 Skipped strings: shells

In the shapes with the root on string 6, the underside of finger 1 (on the root) also touches string 5 to mute it. In the shapes with the root on string 5, the finger on the root leans against string 4.

  • Easy because: three notes, three fingers, and the shapes move anywhere.
  • Hard because: the skipped string must not sound. It is muted by a finger resting on it without pressing, and the strings above the shape are muted too.
  • What goes wrong:
    • The skipped string rings, because the muting finger isn’t touching it.
    • Playing too hard, which brings the muted strings back.

Practice: strum all six strings with the shape held. Only three notes should come out.

Unlocks: Four to the bar, Charleston, and blues for guitar; G-A8.

G-B13 Barre with a skipped string: drop 3

  • Easy because: the shapes are a barre plus at most two notes, and Cm7 is a barre alone.
  • Hard because: you need barre strength, but string 5 under the barre has to be silent. Lift the barre slightly where it crosses string 5 so it only touches the string.
  • What goes wrong:
    • String 5 sounds.
    • String 1 rings.

Practice: play Cm7 alone, then add finger 3 for C7. Then try fingers 3 and 4 together for Cmaj7.

Unlocks: the Drop 3 guitar voicing; G-A11.

G-B14 Drop 2 and extensions: unusual fingerings

Cmaj7 xx2413 is fingered 2-4-1-3. That’s an order the hand hasn’t used before.

  • Easy because: only four strings, close together.
  • Hard because: the fingers come in unusual orders, and some shapes combine a small barre, a skipped string and a stretch of three or four frets.
  • What goes wrong:
    • Hand ache from long sessions.
    • Grabbing the wrong finger.
    • One note losing pressure in the stretch.

Practice: learn one ii–V–I in drop 2, saying the finger numbers out loud. Then move it up two frets.

Unlocks: the Drop 2 voicing, jazz comping, and the altered chords of G-A13.

Where the two sequences meet

Harmonic order By hand
G-A1 Open triads G-B1, G-B2, G-B3 The same chords, sorted by how many fingers they need and how far they reach.
G-A2 Fifths G-B1 E5 is one of the first shapes.
G-A3 Barre chords G-B8, G-B9, G-B10 The barre, then the slide.
G-A4 Sus and add9 G-B2, G-B3 One finger moved.
G-A5 Dominant 7th G-B4, G-B5, G-B11 Open 7ths, then barre 7ths.
G-A6 m7 and maj7 G-B6, G-B11 Small barre, then full barre.
G-A8 Shells G-B12 The first skipped strings.
G-A9 Top-string triads G-B7 Physically easy, but they come later in the harmonic order.
G-A10 Drop 2 G-B14 The hardest fingerings.
G-A11 Drop 3 G-B13 A barre with a skipped string.

The orders differ most in the middle. In the harmonic order a shell (G-A8) is simpler than a full 7th chord. Physically it is harder, because the string between has to be muted. A player who knows G-B4 can try shells with the root on string 6 without learning the barre first.
